post.headline: Where you're born can cost you 20 years of life
post.caption: People in America's richest counties now outlive the poorest by up to 20 years. In Oglala Lakota County, South Dakota, life expectancy is 66.8. In Colorado's Summit County it's 86.9. The richest 1% of men outlive the poorest 1% by 14.6 years.
post.cta: Full story and interactive maps at the link in bio.

cues.text: Where you're born can cost you 20 years of life.
In Oglala Lakota County, South Dakota, life expectancy is just 66.8 years, the lowest in America.
But in Summit County, Colorado, Americans live to 86.9 years, the highest in America.
This is the greatest gap in life expectancy across regions in the last 40 years.
Much of this has to do with wealth. Households in Summit earn 2.5 times more than in Oglala Lakota.
The more money you have, the longer you live. The richest 1% of men outlive the poorest 1% by 14.6 years, and for women it's 10.1.
Data from 1.4 billion tax records reveals a brutal divide. From 2001 to 2014, the richest men gained 2.3 years of life while the poorest gained just a third of a year.
Life expectancy collapse is largely concentrated in the South. Since 1980, 13 counties have seen life expectancy fall, and 8 of them are in Kentucky.
With expensive healthcare in the US, it is hard to get ahead. Healthcare in America costs $10,624 per person, more than double that of the UK, Japan, or Canada.
If Americans cannot afford the cost of healthcare, they are destined to die earlier.
We cannot allow some people to lose 20 years of their life just because they were unlucky enough to be born in one place and not another.
You can read the full story on American Inequality.
